title: CAA-related inflammation (CAA-ri)
consultQuestion: Older patient with subacute cognitive change, seizures, or headache and asymmetric white-matter edema with lobar microbleeds — CAA-ri? Biopsy or treat?
keyHistory: Subacute cognitive or behavioral change (58%), headache (42%), seizure (42%), focal deficit (19%) (Regenhardt)
Known CAA or prior lobar ICH (Auriel)
Anti-amyloid antibody therapy — ARIA has a similar clinicoradiologic picture (Auriel)
Cancer, immunosuppression, infection risk — criteria require excluding neoplastic and infectious causes (Auriel)
redFlags: Declining consciousness or mass effect from edema
Features of lymphoma or infection — steroids can obscure lymphoma (Auriel)
No steroid response within 3 weeks — consider brain biopsy (Auriel)

clues: Asymmetric T2/FLAIR WMH extending to the immediately subcortical white matter plus lobar microbleeds, macrobleed, or cortical superficial siderosis (Auriel)
APOE ε4/ε4 in 77% vs 5% of noninflammatory CAA (Kinnecom)
Extensive WMH is common in noninflammatory CAA — possible criteria only 68% specific (Auriel)

notes: Probable criteria: asymmetric WMH to the immediately subcortical WM (not from past ICH) + ≥1 cortico-subcortical macrobleed, microbleed, or cSS (Auriel Table 1)
Small DWI lesions and gadolinium enhancement are not reliable for diagnosis (Auriel); enhancement in 34% (Regenhardt)

workup.test: LP: cells, protein, glucose, cytology, flow cytometry, infectious studies
notes: CSF protein >45 mg/dL in 92%, cells >5/μL in 26% (Regenhardt)
Neither sensitive nor specific — mainly to exclude mimics (Auriel)

indication: Probable criteria not met or a mimic is suspected
notes: Focal, segmental inflammation can be missed on biopsy (Auriel)

decisionRules.condition: Age ≥40; ≥1 of headache, decreased consciousness, behavioral change, focal signs/seizures (not from acute ICH); asymmetric WMH extending to immediately subcortical WM (not from past ICH); ≥1 cortico-subcortical macrobleed, microbleed, or cSS; no neoplastic, infectious, or other cause
evidenceNote: Auriel 2016 Table 1; 17 pathology-proven cases vs 37 noninflammatory CAA controls

decisionRules.condition: Same, but WMH need not be asymmetric
Empirically treated, no response within 3 weeks

decisionRules.recommendation: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3–5 days, then oral prednisone 60 mg daily tapered over months
evidenceNote: Regenhardt 2020: most common regimen, called reasonable by the authors
Retrospective: improvement 94% treated vs 50% untreated; recurrence 26% vs 71% (HR 0.19)

decisionRules.recommendation: Cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate can be considered — sparse data

initialSteps: Where feasible, exclude lymphoma and infection before empiric steroids (Auriel)
pearls: APOE ε4/ε4: 10/13 (77%) CAA-ri vs 2/39 (5%) noninflammatory CAA, OR 61.7 (Kinnecom); 15/33 (45%) in Regenhardt
Cognition improved and seizures resolved within 1–2 weeks of treatment in responders (Kinnecom)
All symptomatic recurrences in Kinnecom occurred off immunosuppression; one ICH occurred in a region of recurrent hyperintensity
sources: Auriel E, et al. Validation of Clinicoradiological Criteria for the Diagnosis of Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy-Related Inflammation. JAMA Neurol 2016;73:197-202. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2015.4078
Regenhardt RW, et al. Association Between Immunosuppressive Treatment and Outcomes of Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy-Related Inflammation. JAMA Neurol 2020;77:1261-1269. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2020.1782
Kinnecom C, et al. Course of cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related inflammation. Neurology 2007;68:1411-1416
